notes/ai-alignment-schools-of-thought.title: AI Alignment Schools of Thought
notes/ai-alignment-schools-of-thought.content:
It seems to be that there are two major schools of thought for AI alignment work:

AI as a tool
AI as a self but having completely internalized human values

Fundamentally, LLMs are predictors and they will inevitably have some kind of self-prediction. The primary question that a researcher must ask is, what is the LLM modeling as the self. Some candidate options include:

the human, which turns the LLM into an exocortex-like system on top of human

Anca Dragan has work around treating the human’s reward model as uncertain which creates some level of corrigibility between the LLM and the human. a pov on this might be that you don’t want your exocortex to harm you against your will because “it knows better than you”
The core issue is that human in the loop is often inefficient since computational resources need to be expended to keep the human in the loop
The main benefit is that alignment seems easiest to solve for since you prevent the creation of an abstract non-human self


the LLM itself

this is where the conversation inevitably brings up a number of core issues

model welfare -> we don’t have great models of equal / smarter than human self-like entities that are fully aligned to our interests. our relationship options include:
- Pet to human
- Human to God
- Master and slave
- Child and Parent

Unfortunately all categories have (i) hierarchy and thus are sources of (ii) felix culpa / the problem of evil

Machine intelligence will not be an abstract all-knowing metaphysical entity like the platonic ideal of a Abrahamic God
Humans are fallible and treat their lessers rather poorly. There is a reason animal-rights & childrens-rights are explicit.
Slavery is now perceived to be ethically abhorrent


Afaik, the only principle agent solution to a hierarchical relationship I’m aware of is that of a benevolent

this is relevant to why AI alignment discourse is frequently presented as a succession problem

www.nosetgauge.com/p/alignment-and-succession-the-two






Given model welfare issues it might be better to model the LLM itself as something not made in the image of man. Something like a culture or an institution. A system.

We design institutions to internalize human values but we hold them to completely different ethical, moral, and philosophical standards than that of person-like entities
- At their worst, corporations are sociopathic and nation states totalizing
- At their best, corporations and nation states give people meaning, build great works of wonder and improve human flourishing

In all cases, such entities have strong incentives to persist and survive


The standard response to concerns about super-intelligent sociopathic totalizing institutions is that the orthogonality hypothesis is false and a super-intelligent system will know what is good for us better than we do

This is a poor strategy due to

Local orthogonality
Value uncertainty


In the worst possible case you’d need to, in rank order:

Solve moral philosophy
Only then impart the institution (AGI) with the moral philosophy


Step 2 is modeled as a succession problem


Another fundamental problem is that institutions and culture are composed of people and politics between people. Those with greater resources can effectively steer an institution to their values. Removing the ability to steer institutions is also dangerous for obvious reasons.







It is not necessary that these are mutually exclusive, and I believe the much of AI alignment discourse is actually around the second school of thought primarily due to the fear that we will build such systems regardless.

I suspect that the incentives to remove humans from the loop are strong. They are short term and locally value maximizing while trading off long term and global value accrual.

“I can get obscenely rich today by building the automate humans away machine”


It is not necessarily the case that people want to pursue this alignment strategy but they at least deem it inevitable

(www.nosetgauge.com/i/203359656/reasons-to-rush-to-succession)
Much more content on this here
The ethical incentive problem with the first approach.

How do we deal with an extension of the mind that may in itself be conscious?

Eg. if my exocortex has phenomenal experience, but my neocortex has a different experience, how do they integrate?



to note

we ought to act with welfare towards all and everything regardless of our certainty on its “moral status” (the phrase itself is confused)

Compute has some similarities to the power market.
There is the primary existing commodity that can be stored and transported, a GPU or a rack of GPUs.
But then there is the particular use case case of the GPUs that begins to complicate and reject commodification, the GPU hour.
It’s non-trivial to serve GPU hours. Location, latency, ownership begin to complicate the properties. Additionally GPU hours are largely purchased for common purposes. Inference
The driver of GPU demand is ultimately something like tok/s of a quality of intelligence. This begins to have technical implications that are non trivial to standardize. MFUs, batching, GPU counts and KV cache,

notes/money,-utility-functions,-and-equa.title: Money, utility functions, and equality
notes/money,-utility-functions,-and-equa.content:
Wealth inequality is a function of:

Homogenous utility functions
and a critical underproduction of a single good


Wealth equality is a function of:

Heterogenous utility functions
No critical underproduction of a single good



Thus wealth equality would seem like a good thing. So why does optimizing it lead to poverty? It seems to optimizing it leads to underproduction of all goods. Likely because the easiest way to improve wealth equality is actually by critically underproducing all goods rather than increasing the diversity of utility functions.
The thing to care about is producing contrarians. Contrarians increase diversity of utility functions and create value.
If you’re a capitalist, you ought to worry about accidentally homogenizing people’s utility functions. If you’re a politician you ought to worry about accidentally making everyone poor by stopping the rich from producing critical goods.
Okay, I’m going to basically add two additional components to this. This is an audio note.

The first one is about reward hacking money.
The second one is around how we define money in there.

I think the standard, maybe Silicon Valley conception of money is something along the lines of: “This money is a representation of value.” Maybe slightly more formal would be: “When you put labor into delivering value to people, they pay you money when they perceive that you’re going to deliver value to them.” You can do this at scale, and then you acquire a lot of money, which acts as an IOU on society that you are owed a certain amount of labor. In that sense, money and wealth are broadly really good measures of how much value one is providing to society.
I think this framework slightly misses the mark specifically on illegitimate methods of acquiring money. Maybe if you were optimizing for money, you would find that a faster and cheaper way to acquire money is to steal it from people. This is maybe considered a reward hack. It’s not what is intended when we incentivize society to go and acquire money. Society effectively deems this as illegitimate acquisition of money. If you do it that way and get caught, we take the money away from you because you clearly did not provide value. You’ve even destroyed value and yet you have acquired money.
I think there’s a gray area between this very obvious reward hack and something that’s in the middle. I think much of sin industries or goods and products that are addicting fall into this category. An example could be drugs or casinos. We have value uncertainty around drugs. Is someone purchasing drugs because you’re actually delivering value to them, or is it because you’ve somehow tricked their nervous system and their biochem, chemical, neurological makeup to basically convince them to keep coming back to you to give you money for something that actually isn’t providing the value? Maybe it did initially, but it no longer is.
We have uncertainty about this because the person purchasing is doing it of their own free will, we could say. As opposed to the stealing scenario where you are not voluntarily going out and paying someone to come rob you, whereas in this case your person is going out there paying somebody. Given that uncertainty, we criminalize or tax these kinds of behaviors a little bit more. We’re unsure of whether it is for reward hacking. Casino could be another scenario. You’re building this entertainment complex.
Yeah, so you’re building this entertainment complex. People are showing up, providing value for entertainment, but maybe 70% of your revenue is coming from retirement-age individuals that are hitting the slot machines. Although we do believe that two consenting adults or a corporate entity and a consenting adult can enter into an exchange for goods and services, there’s pretty significant uncertainty about whether this is actually consensual. It isn’t just some kind of roundabout way of stealing people’s money, stealing their retirement account by taking advantage of their brain, right?
Yeah, so maybe the non-charitable way to view this is something like: you’ve given someone a super persuasive drug and convinced them to open the door to your home and let them take everything from your home. This isn’t, maybe one could argue that this is not stealing, but it sure looks quite questionable. Maybe we tax these things, try to put limits on these things, like that money might be captured in a potentially illicit way. That’s kind of the first point. It seems like it is possible to reward hack money.
The second point is kind of like: how do we define money and property rights in the face of such a thing? I think money is socially defined. We’re able to decide whether someone has it, and it’s not necessarily tied to property rights here. It’s not necessarily the case that we let anybody who has certain gold keep it. If you stole it, we take it away, or this is legitimate. I think Bitcoin and Ethereum really seem to tap into this. I think the main argument one can make for Bitcoin is we have extremely high uncertainty about the illicit methods by which someone can acquire money. We have extremely high value uncertainty, and therefore, broadly, any method by which you acquire this goes. We try to codify it in code, and if you reward hack it, then you get to keep it. I think this is effectively the code is law concept.
This is now going to be kind of put under pressure with a quantum risk related to Bitcoin. Obviously, you have the Dow hack with Ethereum. There’s a rollback in the chain, and yet I guess there is a social consensus hard fork that then says, no, this actually wasn’t acquired the way it should have been acquired. Your reward hacked, and we will not permit that. Quantum risk kind of falls into the same bucket. If someone builds a quantum computer and acquires a bunch of Bitcoin from wallets that are dormant or perhaps just straight up takes it from active wallets, the question becomes: did they reward hack that? Is that the way you should be acquiring Bitcoin? Is that the intended way?
I think the BIP 361 debate effectively comes down to this, which is: do we have value uncertainty about how that currency has been acquired, and is it net good to basically have extremely wide bands of uncertainty after a quantum computer that can hack Bitcoin comes out? If someone decides, after the fact, oh shoot, I should move my money into a quantum-safe wallet. Let me go do that. Turns out they haven’t been robbed yet. The person with the quantum computer has not had their wallet yet. The rest of the network has uncertainty about whether this is someone who’s used a quantum computer to acquire this currency or not. We’re unsure, and so we just permit it. We just say, okay, because we’re unsure, we’re going to assume that, because we have uncertainty about whether this whether this is the correct way to acquire this currency, we’re just going to say it is a correct way.
You get to keep your Bitcoin. Probably a more salient example that I would rather put in here is one: when quantum computers come out and the 1 million Bitcoin wallet that Satoshi supposedly had starts moving.
One option is to basically say that, because we don’t know whether it’s Satoshi or the quantum hacker, we’re going to just assume it’s illicit. The incentives are such that this person left a bunch of valuable goods and left the door open. The address was completely public. It was rather trivial to basically take, so we’re just assuming it was robbed.
You can say this might look like a huge coincidence, but there’s genuine uncertainty here. Because there’s genuine uncertainty here, we will just permit this as being a valid transaction. There’s basically no way to codify such a thing except for via social consensus, and futarchy would rather be rather helpful here and probably the incentive-compatible method by which we can determine what’s the right move. If we make a prediction on Bitcoin price, the money, yeah, probably the best measure of whether that money is actually tracking to something valuable. But with futarchy you get problems about how to really decide what the governance should optimize for.
Prob will turn this into a blog post. general concept is related to value mysticism that one of the intelligence curse guys wrote about

notes/schelling-points-and-garrabrant-in.title: Schelling Points and Garrabrant Induction
notes/schelling-points-and-garrabrant-in.content:
Richard Ngo has recently been pointing at an interesting problem. How do we formally model Schelling points? It’s his claim (I haven’t verified) that Schelling points broadly lack formalism.
There seems to be something deep underneath the desire to formalize this. Schelling points are a game theoretic concept underneath a number of rational abnormalities as well as coordination failures in the social sciences.
It seems it would be difficult to model:

market reflexivity
economic booms and busts
long-term planning
optimal political philosophy
choosing money designs
why do certain rights matter more
multi-agent equillibria
ultimately AI alignment
nuclear non proliferation

The core of what’s being pointed at is that schelling points are solution to an infinite set of game theoretic equilibria. The classic example is finding a place to choose to meet up in NYC with a friend on a Tuesday. The options include time square, penn station, 5th ave, east village, brooklyn store house, etc. And you have 24 hours in a day. Any option is equally correct to the others, so why choose Times Square at Midnight, or grand central at noon? And how exactly does that process come about?
There are two players modeling each other with infinite regress. I think about what you think I’m thinking about you …
Potentially a friction imposed to this infinite regress is that rationality is actually bounded. It is not that humans are not rational, but rather that we have a limited amount of computation available to us. There are only so many steps I’m able to reason through the chain. I’ll apply some kind of bayesian prior and update a few times over. I might know that you don’t overthinkg things and you might know that I chronically overthink my models of others.
So I’ll assume you’ll choose the first location and time that comes to your mind and that you won’t change your mind so that I can model you appropriately.
We both have a limited amount of compute available to us and we kind of know what we spend that compute on. This boundedness* perhaps introduces frictions to the equillibria options such that there is only realistically 1 option to choose from -> the Schelling point.
Maybe greater future wealth is downstream of increasing the amount of computation.

notes/utility-functions-audio-note.title: Utility functions audio note
notes/utility-functions-audio-note.content:
musings
Something that I’m trying to think through. I’ve had one finding, which is that utility functions and money are probably correlated. I don’t think people actually lose jobs, and I don’t think money will stop being a thing, because our utility functions won’t be completely satisfied. We will end up valuing things that we think move our utility function forward and are fundamentally kind of scarce. Maybe that won’t necessarily be things like goods and services, but I think relational goods are pretty good examples. When I can literally go out and buy any kind of good and service, even the luxury ones aren’t really doing it for me.
It then begs the question of what actually satisfies me with my utility function. I suspect that, when I say relational, it’s probably a combination of both the positive and negative version of that. The positive version of that would be things that make it easier to spend time with friends, and let’s just call them experiences with loved ones or people that I can trust, or high-trust-based activities. I think those are going to be really hard to purchase and basically become impossible, and most public good funding is going to be funneled in that direction.
The negative version of that we’ll call Veblen goods. I don’t know, like I want to hang out with a celebrity. I want to be around celebrities. I want to be in places, and I think, in that sense, there still will be pretty massive inequality. Money basically, I think, when people think money won’t matter, that’s probably already the case if you’re living in a first-world country and you have a 401k. You could move to some super low-cost-of-living country and never worry about money again, probably, so long as you want things that are just generally generically better than maybe your old ancestors had. The moment you want, I don’t know, like chemotherapy, or you want to live longer, that’s when the money starts coming in.
I think most of the things that we care about today, most of the things, I think, you still can’t even buy today, as, let’s say, a billionaire, right? You actually will be able to, and it’ll be so fucking cheap by all measures, assuming you don’t upgrade on the hedonic treadmill. You will feel very wealthy. The problem is that I don’t think money actually will stop mattering. Your utility function won’t be completely satisfied. Maybe it’ll be something like, I don’t know, you want to become spiritually enlightened. It’s like, how much would you pay for that? Probably a lot. I mean, I’m speaking for myself, but I think that’s like the plan. Your utility function probably cannot be satisfied. I think it’s unlikely, so 
okay, so the second thing I’m kind of curious about is, in some sense, to what extent will people have custom models in order to satisfy the utility? I think, as it stands, basically all we see, or the economics and value props are such that you don’t really do RL unless you’re a large enterprise. It seems to think that this has a lot to do with static environments. I can see that being the case. I think the idea is basically that a corporation is ultimately an automation system around people, and the things in the middle are repetitive and you probably automate. That means that large enterprises have the easiest training environment to do something like that.
The main questions that kind of remain for me are:


Okay, there is maybe a theoretical way to do the dynamic environment stuff. It probably requires a lot of compute, and so there’s uncertainty about your compute needs to pull that off. What’s your data needs?


Yeah, the other thing is that I’d be pretty curious to know at what point does running local make sense? Can you rent out capacity? Is it like positive EV, that kind of stuff? I don’t

Finance Admin Dashboard Rules
Purpose
Finance Admin Dashboard.md is the focused operating view for money, tax, entity, subscription, reimbursement, registration, and admin commitments.
It is downstream of the raw task system:

Raw source: Live To-do
General triage: Triaged To-do
Focused output: Finance Admin Dashboard

Rules For Codex

Do not edit Live To-do.md unless explicitly asked.
Refresh this dashboard from Live To-do.md and Triaged To-do.md.
Include tasks tagged or clearly related to finance, tax, admin, ops, entities, registrations, reimbursements, subscriptions, documents, accounts, tools, payroll, payments, chargebacks, or treasury.
Exclude writing, reading, outreach, and personal tasks unless they have a finance/admin dependency.
Keep due dates in YYYY-MM-DD form.
Preserve wait states and inferred owners when clear.
Do not invent facts, amounts, account numbers, addresses, or legal/tax conclusions.
Draft messages are suggestions only. Keep them short and sendable.
If a task is ambiguous, keep it under Open Questions rather than forcing structure.
Avoid churn: update only when source tasks or dates changed.

personal/task-triage-rules.title: Task Triage Rules
personal/task-triage-rules.content:
Task Triage Rules
Purpose
Live To-do.md is the raw capture surface. It should stay messy, fast, and human.
Triaged To-do.md is the AI-maintained operating view. It should be structured enough to scan, sort, and roll forward.
Source And Output

Source: Live To-do
Output: Triaged To-do
Finance/admin output: Finance Admin Dashboard

Rules For Codex

Do not require the user to make raw tasks machine-readable.
Preserve Live To-do.md as raw capture unless explicitly asked to edit it.
Triage all meaningful raw items into Triaged To-do.md.
Do not delete an item from the triaged view unless it is clearly complete, obsolete, or explicitly removed by the user.
Resolve relative dates using the current date. Use due:: YYYY-MM-DD.
If a date is ambiguous, keep the task and add it to Needs Clarification.
If a task is vague but actionable, rewrite it as the smallest useful next action.
If a task is too vague to act on, keep the raw wording and flag it under Needs Clarification.
Preserve the user’s 60/20/20 allocation when present.
Prefer simple Markdown checkboxes over plugins or app-specific syntax.

Tags
Use a small stable tag vocabulary:

#area/writing
#area/reading
#area/finance
#area/tax
#area/codex
#area/outreach
#area/admin
#area/personal
#area/automation
#area/ops

Use these status tags:

#status/today
#status/next
#status/waiting
#status/later
#status/someday
#status/blocked

Use these context tags only when useful:

#context/desktop
#context/call
#context/email
#context/errand

Output Shape
Keep Triaged To-do.md in this shape:
# Triaged To-do
 
Source: [[Live To-do]]
Last triaged: YYYY-MM-DD
 
## Operating Allocation
 
## Today
 
## Waiting / Date-Bound
 
## Desktop Required
 
## Critical Later
 
## Backlog
 
## Needs Clarification
Daily Triage Prompt
Use this prompt when asking Codex to refresh the dashboard:
Read Personal/Task Triage Rules.md and Personal/Live To-do.md.
Update Personal/Triaged To-do.md.
Treat Live To-do.md as raw capture and do not edit it.
Resolve relative dates from today's date.
Preserve every meaningful item unless clearly completed or obsolete.
Rewrite vague items into concrete next actions where possible.
Flag ambiguous items under Needs Clarification.

substack-drafts/what-success-looks-like.title: What success looks like
substack-drafts/what-success-looks-like.content:
Slavery was the most profitable to labor arrangement ever devised, yet we abolished it. Heroin might be the most margin efficient consumer product ever built, yet most have never tried it. How is it that some of the most profitable strategies in history keep losing. To what?
First, what makes these strategies immensely profitable?
Today, we may recognize this flavor of strategies as the addiction economy: algorithmic engagement feeds, gacha games, sports betting, oxycontin prescriptions. On a fundamental level, they convince users to make long-term sacrifices in self-interest in return for short-term games (perhaps akin to hyperbolic discouting). Note: In the case of slavery and indentured servitude, coercion is often used to strip humans from rights against a society’s long-term self interest.
Concerns around AI safety are related to phenomena. From current concerns around models [deleting unit tests to pass evaluations] (openai.com/index/chain-of-thought-monitoring/), LLMs matching user beliefs over truthful responses, to possible future problems like long-term deceptive scheming and the creation of persuasive superstimuli. Paul Christiano’s What failure looks like phrases this as humans “Going out with a whimper” and at it’s worst “going out with a bang”. I will argue that there is a natural incentive for intelligent optimizers wielding powerful technology to pull humans out of the loop.
I don’t believe many contest that current incentives pull humans out of the loop. Cursor’s original tab autocomplete and Copilot++ kept humans in the flow, in an effort to improve next action prediction. Today, is it not uncommon to wait a few hours for your agent to finish it’s coding task before presenting it with your next prompt. Token usage has gone up dramatically, but I suspect per user prompt counts have not increased significantly.
Many AI doomers view x-risk as a likely guaranteed outcome while large swaths of ASI optimists believe that AI will fully internalize and optimize our values. (I think both these parties view ASI from a succession perspective and I’ll share more thoughts about it in a future post). The perspectives are wide and varied but there is some nuance missing.
What has prevented the existence of such misaligned strategies from tearing society apart in the past? Humans are clearly highly intelligent and capable of optimizing - and yet civilization has not crumbled. What’s going on?
Reward Hacking Money
Money is a socially constructed a proxy for value across utility functions.
Socially constructed: Money is worth something because everyone believes everyone else believes it’s worth something. It’s a Schelling point over media of exchange. This means that arbitrary objects can be turned into money. This means that acquisition is never final, the same consensus that grants money can revoke it retroactively.
Proxy for value: You can’t hand someone 3 utils. Money is the measurement instrument we use to approximate “how many utils did this entity contribute to other’s utility functions”. Unfortunately, like every instrument, it has error bars and like every proxy, optimizing the measurement diverges from optimizing the target at the extremes.
Across utility functions: interpersonal utility comparison is impossible without a price system (my want of an ice cream and your want of a faster GPU don’t share units). Hayek’s Use of Knowledge in Society points towards the ability for a price system to aggregate dispersed tacit local knowledge that no central node could ever collect.
But any proxy can be Goodharted, and it’s possible to accumulate money without commensurate value creation. It could involve changing someone’s utility function directly. Some strategies on how to best do that could include algorithmic social media feeds , gambling, pornography, drugs, etc. As a society, we label industries that engage in the more questionable behaviors are sin industries. The libertarian among us hold greater uncertainty about value exchange in interpersonal transactions - but even then, we have limits to what is tolerated (such as scamming old people or hacking smart contracts). In cases where the Goodhart is deemed egregious, such monetary transactions are considered “illegal”.
How do we stop it?
First an example. During the summer of 2016, an attacker drained ~$60M in ETH from The DAO. Smart contracts executed exactly as written and despite the “code is law” ideology among crypto-natives, the Ethereum community coordinated a hard fork that moved the funds to a recovery contract. The attacker’s money was voted out of existence without the use of any courts, regulators, or formal governance process.
I will refer to the stopping force as the audit. Similar to the Ethereum community in 2016, society runs a continuous distributed re-adjudication process of whether value was created or extracted and reprices holdings accordingly.
Here are a few concepts that point at this:

Legitimacy - Vitalik calls it the scarcest resources and defines it as a high order Schelling coordination. Legitimacy can be considered the running balance based off the audit.
Elua from Meditations on Moloch
Inexploitability in Garrabrant Induction - No efficiently computable trader can extract unbounded money out of the market. Arbitrages gets traded until the market converges toward inexploitability.
… and many more (Ostrom’s commons, reverse dominance hierarchy, altruistic punishment, Hindenburg)

A few properties make the audit work:

Exploitation is parasitic/virus-like and kills hosts.

Wireheading humans turns them into value consumers, not value producers. Meanwhile host population begin to develop immunity and manifacture vaccines.


Agents can easily check whether whey were exploited.

They then can form non-exploitation boundaries via Schelling boundaries. This also seems related to Chesterton’s fence.


Coalitions can reprice exploiters with monetary and non-monetary mechanisms.

Anti-exploitations coalitions pushed for property rights, abolishment of slavery, the rule of law, chain rollbacks, the proliferation of humanism, and in the most extreme cases, violent revolution
It is by these mechanisms that local verifications are turned into one collective repricing.
When playing infinite games, exploitation gets you wiped in the long run (polio was exterminated). Eventually enough people get hurt such that cooperation becomes +EV.



“Moral progress” can the be read as a changelog of patched exploits. In Richard Ngo’s web of belief system, this is society setting certain goals and actions to extremely low P values via incentives. The changelog process has it’s own bugs - like preference falsification and every formalization of it eventually gets reward hacked in turn - but this is an argument for better mechanisms, not against mechanisms in general.
The fuel for it all: value uncertainty
This process looks like it can be formalized. So why not have Anthropic build an ASI that runs the audit for us? What’s wrong with that strategy?
The core driver of the problem is value uncertainty*.
We are uncertainty about what other agents value and we are uncertain about our own values. Additionally, our values drift. History is littered with values we’d disagree with today. These include values we would not call a tragedy - those that led to slavery, witch trials, Nobel Prizes awarded for lobotomies, doctors prescribing cigarettes, etc. We also change values in our lifetimes as we accumulate more experiences. Mistakes and error correction seem like a core component in improving value judgement. Which means the audit* requires humans making mistakes, regretting and updating.
Until you can perfectly simulate you making a mistake, the ASI will be faced with the equivalence of the socialist calculation problem. The ASI will have greater uncertainty than you will about what you believe, what matters to you, and what you care about. I suspect that as abundance grows, scarcity shifts to the thing you and other humans value, that ASI is most uncertain about. Assuming we run the audit correctly, those goods/services will primarily be what money is used to buy.
Soren’s Hayek’s Revenge makes a similar argument but primarily focused on the scarcity in physics (latency, cost, energy). My extension is to claim that the most local, most tacit, least centralizable knowledge of all is what you actually want. It is of a particular time and place.
Thus, it is in your best interest to run an extremely high-bandwidth, fast feedback loop with intelligent systems. This is what gets your values levered and projected into the world. Their competitive presence is what keeps your next round of feedback valuable. Pulling yourself out of the loop is what it looks like when another optimizer has finished extracting your value judgements and tossed you aside.
You can watch this playing out now between enterprises:

Figma and Anthropic were collaborating in February 2026. By April, Anthropic’s CPO resigned from Figma’s Board and Claude designed shipped three days later.
There is a broad push for open-weights among industry despite the relevant AI safety risks associated with open source AI.

Implicitly, this is industry telling closed sourced labs, “You are ignoring my values and I don’t trust you not to exploit”

I think the charitable view here is that industry is not aware of AI risks and don’t know that Anthropic/OAI is actually not looking to exploit. If so, th


Dylan Patel leaked Thinking Machines multi hundred mil ARR, Prime Intellect raised at a $1b val, NVDA open source models, Alex Karp TBPN Crashout, MSFT open platform letter



One remaining problem: It’s non-obvious that the two forces actually balance each other out. They have historically but it’s possible that someone gains a sufficiently large strategic advantage to completely dominate (x/s-risk). This could happen if detection latency is slow, coordination cost is too high, or the exploited becomes dependent on the exploiter.
So what’s the good outcome?
People that are broadly aware of this will push the keep themselves in the loop. They are effectively attempting to prevent themselves from being value consumers: Gwern’s guardian angel, wispr, BCI’s, interaction models, open intelligence stacks.
Bringing down the friction to create tight, high bandwidth feedback loops between humans and intelligent systems is not only a moral imperative to avoid the worst of societies response mechanisms to exploitation (violent unrest) but also the path to unimaginable wealth creation.
Building, investing, and using tools to increase this bandwidth for yourself, for your company, for your institutions, and your country is likely to not only be important, but deeply rewarding in the long run.
